awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  Zernike Double-Metalens Cooke Triplet
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial impacts of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project are in developing a groundbreaking architecture for thermal imaging lenses that are smaller, lighter, less expensive, and use abundant semiconductor materials such as silicon. This innovation aims to reduce the size and weight of traditional commercial thermal lenses by a factor of two, leveraging new advancements in nanotechnology. The innovation will enhance scientific and technological understanding by offering a mathematical solution to key practical issues. The first market segment targeted is thermal imaging for unmanned aerial vehicles in defense and security applications, using a business-to-business model. This advancement would not only strengthen the U.S.'s leadership in optics and innovation but also support new engineering, scientific, and manufacturing capabilities. The project aligns with national priorities, such as those supported by the CHIPS Act, by leveraging existing infrastructure. Additionally, this project will contribute to workforce development by training a diverse group of students in cutting-edge STEM fields. The proposed technology will provide a durable competitive advantage and be a key factor in enabling the commercial success of the innovation.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project seeks to address key technical challenges that have limited the practical application of flat lenses in commercial imaging systems. The primary research objectives are to determine whether the proposed Zernike Double Metalens Cooke Triplet can simultaneously eliminate both image noise and chromatic aberration, achieving high-quality imaging with much fewer optical elements to gain superiority over size and weight when compared to commercial lenses. This will mark a breakthrough in lens architecture with flat optics, moving the technology from research labs to real-world applications. One of the objectives is to mathematically solve a highly non-linear system of coupled equations using a mix of several algorithms to obtain a feasible solution for addressing the undesired large chromatic aberration in flat lens design while keeping a high efficiency. Another objective is to eliminate image noise with the proposed unique architecture while still maintaining a practically feasibly optical system for harsh environments. The project will advance a first prototype in collaboration with payload developers in the aerial imaging systems. The successful completion of this R&D effort will lay the foundation for further commercialization, with the ultimate goal of integrating the technology into commercial imaging sensors.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Advancing Thermal Imaging with Innovative Metalens Technology

Thermal imaging cameras detect heat to "see" in complete darkness, through smoke or fog, making them essential for farming, security patrols, industrial checks (like power lines or pipelines), and defense operations. Traditional thermal lenses are heavy, thick, and expensive because they need many glass pieces to create clear pictures and fix issues like color blur (chromatic aberration) that ruin image quality.

In this NSF SBIR Phase I project, Corlens Inc. created a new hybrid lens system called the Zernike Double-Metalens Cooke Triplet. It combines one regular front lens with two super-thin "metalenses": flat surfaces covered in millions of tiny silicon pillars that bend light precisely. This design, inspired by an early lab discovery of sharper images from a special setup, uses math-based patterns (Zernike polynomials) to cancel out light aberrations. The goal: build a simpler, much lighter system that could replace complex 10+ element lenses, cutting size, weight, and cost while keeping high performance. This innovation directly addresses barriers in metalens technology for real-world use, focusing on long-wave infrared (LWIR) wavelengths from 8 to 12 microns.

Corlens ran detailed computer simulations on over 40 design options, proving the idea works in theory. The top design delivered excellent sharpness across a wide view, with minimal blur, reaching "diffraction-limited" quality (the best possible given light's nature). Metrics showed the designed performance matching or exceeding conventional systems. Corlens then moved to real prototypes: designed the pillar patterns using specialized software, fabricated the metalenses on silicon wafers with about 5.5 million nanostructures each, and tested them in a new lab with a thermal camera sensor (FLIR Boson+). Tests confirmed focusing worked but showed fixable issues like missing anti-reflection coatings causing ghost images and low light transmission (down to 25% efficiency), plus slight pillar tapering from nanomanufacturing that shifted focus slightly. Electron microscope imaging verified pillar heights at 12 microns as designed but revealed a taper, leading to plans for fabrication-aware adjustments in a next phase.

These results advanced science by showing how metalenses can team up with regular lenses in practical ways to beat their usual limits, like noise and color issues in thermal wavelengths. This contributes to the field of photonics and advanced materials by introducing a hybrid architecture that leverages Zernike-based phase control for aberration correction, enabling diffraction-limited imaging across broad fields. It also highlights the importance of integrating simulation with real-world fabrication, identifying second-order effects like stray light and sidewall angles that impact performance. Such insights pave the way for better photonic engineering tools and manufacturing processes, aligning with NSF's emphasis on advancing critical technologies through fundamental research.

The bigger benefits are huge and align closely with NSF priorities in critical and emerging technologies, such as advanced materials, advanced manufacturing, and microelectronics. By engineering metasurfaces on silicon, a widely available semiconductor material, this work strengthens U.S. supply chains and reduces dependence on rare imports like germanium, which face global shortages. It promotes innovation in advanced manufacturing by developing nanostructure libraries informed by fabrication realities, potentially improving yields and scalability for optics production. In terms of national security and economic competitiveness, enhanced thermal imaging supports defense applications like reconnaissance and secure communications equipment, where our undoped silicon upgrades could minimize interference. For agriculture, a key biotech-adjacent area, farmers could use these systems for early detection of crop stress via heat patterns, boosting yields and sustainability.

A smaller, lighter thermal camera means longer drone flights without draining batteries fast or overloading the craft. Drones could carry affordable, high-quality thermal imagers for precision farming (spotting sick crops early by heat differences), security and border monitoring, wildfire detection, or defense reconnaissance. Our customer interviews (over 100 via NSF I-Corps) showed strong demand from drone users in agriculture, security, and defense, especially avoiding rare materials like germanium that have supply problems. Our silicon-based approach helps U.S. innovation and reduces import reliance. It is expected to create jobs in advanced optics, foster public-private partnerships for commercialization, and enhance STEM education by demonstrating accessible nanotechnology. Overall, this project exemplifies NSF's goal of translating basic research into technologies that drive economic growth, secure national interests, and benefit society broadly.

Phase I proved the concept through simulations and first prototypes, while spotting and planning fixes for key hurdles (like better coatings, upgraded wafers, and fabrication tweaks). This greatly lowers risks for next steps, de-risking development in line with NSF's focus on innovation ecosystems. A Phase II would allow Corlens to build improved beta versions, verify phase profiles with specialized equipment, measure full-system chromatic performance, and test in real drone setups, all to bring compact, efficient thermal imaging to drones and other uses for safer, smarter operations in everyday and critical fields.
